en: If the destroyer Manas is born,
Nothing to turn a horse-catching pole will remain.
When Manas comes forth to fight,
No mortal can face him;
Nothing to turn a horse-catching pole will remain,
When Manas rises, no soul will remain.
That Manas will be born among the Burut,
In the Muslim faith;
I speak the truth without distortion:
He is Beijing's enemy by nature.
He will gird on an unsheathed sword;
That bastard, that fierce wolf,
Will turn his wrath outward.
Drinking blood, he will never be sated;
He will spare no one he faces.
High-browed, full of menace,
He has a mark upon his back:
A dark blue-black mane.
His supporters are a host of khojas,
His true companions the forty chiltens.
If that Manas is born,
Will he not unleash fierce wrath,
Will he not exact vengeance far and wide,
On Beijing with its kakan?
Of the Chinese with rank buttons on their caps,
Will he not slaughter the finest?
Making a spectacle of the Chinese,
He will lay many against the earth;
Those who meet his wrath
He will drench in bright red blood.
Will any person survive?
If we live, we shall see
The child whose name is Manas.
He will make you drink bitterness.
Putting your salt into food,
If that Manas grows up,
If you live, you will see:
He will plunder and destroy,
Seize your daughters with their five forelocks,
Burn your city of Beijing,
Smash every one of you.
If that Manas attacks,
He surely will not let us prosper,
Never will he leave us whole.
Your khan with a rank button on his cap,
Your city he will shatter.
He will enslave your men with forelocks,
Your strong men wearing jackets
He will tread into wool beneath his feet.
He will descend upon your heads;
If the bloodthirsty Burut grows up,
He will scatter your four kinds of stock.
Take heed, my khan, prepare;
If you lie about without taking heed,
Tomorrow you will see,
My khan, the smoke entering your eyes.
Braid the mane of your thoroughbred;
If you do not attend to this affair,
Within some ten years
You will see the fierce champion Manas
Here in Beijing!
If that Manas grows up,
He will raid your horses;
May I be denied my portion if I lie,
He will scatter your sleep like crumbled dough.
When the spring days come,
Leaving you no maned mare to ride,
In Kakan Khan's Beijing
He is the man who will cause uproar.
I speak: the calamity is known.
‘The famous hero Manas will arise
And call Beijing to account,’
Is written in the great register before you.
What I say is learned by heart;
Calamity has set out for Beijing.
‘Of Beijing, untouched by Solomon,
He will seize the throne’—
The name of Manas
Has been entered in your book.
The first of the horrors is known:
‘His name is Manas, the fierce wolf,’
My lord, it is written in your bootay.
I saw it in the register and grieved.
Of such a great city
You are ruler, Esenkan;
My lord, I ran to you.
The dream I saw turned ill;
My lord, my Esenkan, listen:
What a calamity this Manas is!
If mighty Manas is born,
He bears the famed name Manas;
There is a written entry in the book.
When I read that writing,
My lord, my ribs tremble.
The reason they tremble—
He is the lion named Manas,
Not only the Chinese, but the peoples of the world
He is the lion who will slaughter.
Such are the troubles heard of him;
He has a horse no shot can reach,
He has a coat no shot can pierce.
The fierce lion Manas,
Drinking blood, will never be sated;
Not only the Chinese, but the peoples of the world—
If born, he will spare no soul.
Mighty in spirit, great in name,
He is the champion, he is the strength.
This Beijing with its kakan,
Your land the Flood could not enter—
He is the man who will throw it into turmoil.
If that hero Manas arises among the Burut,
The whole world cannot overcome him in combat,
A lion's teeth cannot pierce him.
Naked Kydyr is his companion;
Each one is a hero equal to Manas,
His companions come from forty places,
The forty have forty different origins;
All forty are chosen from the world's peoples,
Distinguished champions.
If those forty unite,
Great sorrow will fall on the Chinese;
Beyond the Chinese, that Manas
Will bring great strife to the world's peoples.
If forty leopards unite,
Can any man bring them low?
Can any who meets them remain alive?
Make preparations now,
Send out your discerning men,
Have him driven here to Beijing,
My lord, the child named Manas.
A great dungeon forty rope-lengths deep—
Let us put him in that pit in the earth.
If one named Manas is born,
Let us deal with him this way!”
Of such a great city
Esenkan was ruler;
He had reached exactly a hundred years.
Karykan in Beijing,
When he heard Manas's name,
This Chinese man's heart grew troubled.
The drum was loudly beaten,
A beacon was lit outside.
Karykan and Esenkan,
All these men heard the news;
They sounded shrill copper pipes,
Assembling with drums and shawms,
Hearing the sorcerer's words,
Hearing, “The renowned Manas
Will be born among the Burut.”
The news they had heard,
They saw within the register.
Of the Manchus who could read,
After seeing it in the book,
Exactly twelve died.
Dust flew, birch bark burned,
The city's interior was trampled.
They summoned the sorcerer,
Commanded him and looked:
“One named Manas will be born,”
That bastard had already been
Entered in the book.
It was known he was a lion;
Seven years before his birth,
In Beijing with its kakan
He was written in the book.
Turmoil began;
Great Beijing with its kakan,
When it heard Manas's name,
Fell into confusion.
Karykan in Beijing,
When he heard Manas's name,
The great khan's heart grew troubled.
The golden throne in Beijing,
Surrounded by a grove of plane trees,
No mortal had looked upon;
No person without ablution approached it.
In the time of Prophet Noah,
That was the place where light was shed;
Its khan was called Kakan,
That was the land that stood unbroken.
Until the Day of Judgment,
That was the people who would not waver.
Karykan's golden throne—
Surrounded by a towering grove.
Though soaked in water forty years,
Not the slightest bit would fade;
Though soaked in water eighty years,
Not a shred would rot—
Of carpets patterned in gold,
Sixty were spread out.
Above them stood the golden throne,
No one had fathomed its design,
No person had approached it;
Every mortal who saw it marveled.
Its pillars were gold and diamonds;
Where a person sat upon it,
Rubies and pearls were mingled.
Then Karykan's
Fierce heart grew troubled.
His champion wearing protective armor,
Once his khan gave the command,
The forty doors in Kakan's palace
He opened in a row.
The kettledrum was loudly beaten;
There were forty sorcerers,
Bending their knees to the earth.
Taking clubs as big as houses,
His champions ran,
Every champion gathered
And came before the khan.
Karykan raged:
“My champions, every one of you listen!
Extraordinary executioners and sorcerers,
Long-eared elders, listen!
His forefathers are Burut;
The hero Manas has been born
Among the people called Burut.
Khan of the countless Torgut, come!
Sorcerers, discerning men, all come!
A thousand of you learned men, come!
Serve me well this time.
If there is a boy named Manas,
Go look among those Burut,
Younger than seventeen,
Older than half a year.
If there is a boy named Manas,
Bind his hands and feet and bring him;
Without fail, drive him here;
Without leaving him alive, simply
Drive him this way!
Damn your father's grave, my champion!
If you do not find that Manas,
Do not show yourself before my eyes,
Do not come near me!
Do not appear in my city!
Damn your fathers' graves, champions,
Die before you come to me!
If you do not find that Manas,
I will put a kook upon your heads,
Make every one of you cringe,
Teach you terrible humiliation.
I will make your bare heads ache,
Question your age till you shudder.
If you do not find that Manas,
Binding ropes around your necks,
I will hang you all together.
If you do not find and bring Manas,
Laying punishment on your necks,
I will shoot every last one of you.
I will do as I please;
Leaving none of you alive,
I will slaughter all of you entirely.
If you do not find and bring Manas,
I will have you dealt with;
There are very many swordsmen:
I will have the whole lot of you cut down!”
